item.title: Exploring Collaborative Debating Models for the future of science
item.description: arXiv:2611.00370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI is expanding what researchers can produce. A substantial increase in scientific output would also change how that work is organised and distributed, as earlier shifts in the scale of science have done. This paper develops a thought experiment around Collaborative Debating Models (CDMs), topic-focused environments where researchers work with AI and one another to pursue questions and maintain an evolving account of their field. Individual contributions would remain attributable as ongoing debate and further analysis change the shared account. The paper considers how journals could evolve into these gathering places and how different forms of ownership would shape scientific agendas and the support for continuing work. CDMs could connect participants to remote laboratories and other research services to conduct new studies, with shared repositories making the resulting data available for further inquiry. The proposal links expanded scientific production to collective interpretation through continuing assessment and revision, while leaving room for disciplinary differences in how contributions are reviewed and recognised.
item.dc:creator: Zeki C. Seskir

item.title: Siting and Curtailment Depth Limit the Grid Headroom Available to New Large Loads
item.description: arXiv:2611.00462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data center demand is increasing faster than generation can be built, encouraging proposals to interconnect large loads on condition that they reduce consumption during high-stress periods. Estimates of how much load can be added via flexibility rest on simplified accounting and report only annual curtailed electricity. Here we use a national energy systems model that co-optimizes hourly generation and load curtailment across 16 U.S. regions to characterize the flexibility and power system impacts of enabling headroom. While 50 GW can be served while curtailing less than 0.1% of its annual energy, small annual curtailment conceals potentially severe operating requirements. Most regions require curtailment deeper than 90% in at least one hour, so the load must disconnect or have sufficient on-site resources to provide full back up. Furthermore, announced data center locations are not aligned with modeled headroom and relying on existing generation fleets raises CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity prices.
item.dc:creator: Nils Johnson, Geoff Blanford, John E. T. Bistline

item.title: Optimal Strategies to Contain and Prevent the Spread of Diseases in Group-structured Populations
item.description: arXiv:2611.01341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The strength and speed of an epidemic process in a multiplex network is affected by how modular the networks in each layer are. However, it is not obvious how the dynamics of the spreading process change when the group structure and membership varies between layers. In this work, we demonstrate that restructuring the organization of groups within a population can be used as an effective strategy to decrease the severity of an epidemic. Specifically, we show that when group structures are sufficiently correlated outbreaks are longer but milder than for uncorrelated group structures. Further, we find that random immunization decreases the outbreak size and peak infected values to a greater extent than in correlated groups when compared to random immunization in the uncorrelated, normal assignments. Finally, we investigate the effectiveness of targeted immunization strategies on networks with correlated and uncorrelated group structures. We show that immunizing nodes based on their centrality ranking decreases the size of outbreaks compared to random immunization, and that immunizing central nodes in a correlated network helps to decrease the outbreak size more quickly than in uncorrelated networks.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Resilient Complex Adaptive Systems (eds C. Szabo, R. Castro, V. Semeshenko and S. Mittal) 2026
item.dc:creator: Varun K. Rao, Siddharth Patwardhan, Filippo Radicchi

item.title: Discovering hierarchical governing equations for community-structured complex network dynamics with LLM agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.02816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Governing equations provide an interpretable description of the mechanisms underlying complex network dynamics, yet their discovery from observational data remains challenging when shared community-level dynamics coexist with individual-level variations and the relevant functional structures may be absent from the initial candidate library or not explicitly specified in advance. Here we formulate this task as a hierarchical law-discovery problem and introduce SAGE, a large language model-guided self-reflective agent framework for discovering community-shared governing laws and individual-specific dynamical variations. SAGE organizes equation discovery into an iterative Library-Discovery-Review process that first identifies shared community-level structures and then resolves node-specific residual dynamics, while adaptively refining the candidate space to introduce missing dynamical terms when needed. This hierarchical and interpretable formulation enables SAGE to distinguish shared community-level dynamics from individual-level variations and to reveal the mechanisms underlying complex network dynamics. Across two synthetic networks and four real-world networks spanning mobile communication, brain electrophysiology, power grids and urban rail transit, SAGE recovers compact and interpretable governing equations, reproduces observed system dynamics and outperforms representative equation-discovery baselines. The framework remains robust under incomplete observations and can transfer community-level governing laws to nodes with entirely missing observations. These results establish a hierarchical and adaptive approach for disentangling shared and individual dynamical mechanisms in community-structured complex networks.
item.dc:creator: Jinlei Zhang, Zixuan Zhang, Hao Qiu, Feng Chen, Jiateng Yin, Xiaoyong Yan, Xiaolei Ma, Hao Sun, Jianxi Gao, Lixing Yang, Ziyou Gao

item.title: Zero-shot time-series foundation models against the Khepri v1.5 baselines for 96-hour carbon-intensity forecasts in nine Nordic bidding zones: a preregistered comparison
item.description: arXiv:2611.02895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compare three zero-shot time-series foundation models (Timestral-5M, Timestral-209M and Chronos-2, 8192-hour context, no covariates) with the Khepri v1.5 SARIMA and GBM baselines, with their code and hyperparameters unchanged, for 96-hour forecasts of hourly carbon intensity in the Nordic bidding zones NO1-NO5 and SE1-SE4. The design, the analysis code and a minimum detectable effect (MDE) were timestamped before any foundation-model forecast by an OpenTimestamps proof (Bitcoin-confirmed) and the GPG-signed tag prereg-v1; the proofs are archived in Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23881315). The preregistration was also submitted to OSF Registries 2026-11-02 07:49 UTC (osf.io/hncz5; embargo requested, pending OSF approval). On the 2025 test (361 daily origins, contamination not ruled out) all three models have a lower zone-averaged MAPE than both baselines, by 0.952 to 1.347 percentage points (Diebold-Mariano with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction, all p < 0.0001), and each beats SARIMA in 9 of 9 zones. On a post-release holdout of 14 origins from 2026-10-16 the point estimates have the same sign (0.729 to 1.326 percentage points lower), but all lie within the preregistered MDE of 2.989 points and are reported as not determined. For calibration (RQ4) the preregistration locked a Diebold-Mariano-HLN test on CRPS; the MDE applies to MAPE only. Holdout CRPS point estimates (n = 14) are 1.1114 (Timestral-5M), 1.0733 (Timestral-209M) and 1.1198 (Chronos-2) against 1.4165 gCO2-eq/kWh for SARIMA (each p < 0.0001). The SARIMA quantiles are constructed from the fitted model's Gaussian predictive distribution (deviation D-03), not taken from a native v1.5 forecast, so the difference may partly reflect the SARIMA intervals. The contamination indicator does not exceed its preregistered threshold for any comparison; with 14 holdout origins it has low power (HAC standard errors 0.124 to 0.360 pp).
item.dc:creator: Eirik Botten Nicolaysen

item.title: Algorithmic Intervention Decreases Polarization in Content Moderation
item.description: arXiv:2611.03072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crowd-based moderation relies on people's collective judgments to combat misinformation, but raters bring their own ideological biases to the task, shaping how they moderate each other's contributions. We ask whether an algorithmic redesign can counteract this bias, using X's Community Notes, where contributors write context for potentially misleading posts and rate each other's notes. Community Notes replaced simple majority voting with an algorithm that instead rewards agreement across people with different ideological viewpoints. Comparing 8,805 notes and 4,367 contributors before and after this change, we find that ideological polarization decreased in the algorithm's estimates of contributor and note positions. Although negative interactions increased, contributors became less structurally aligned, indicating that negative interactions were less organized along partisan lines. These findings show that algorithmic incentives can reshape both the social structure and behavioral dynamics of crowds, extending beyond their intended effects on content moderation.
item.dc:creator: Anna Bertani, Saeedeh Mohammadi, Taha Yasseri

item.title: When will androids outnumber humans?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humanoid robots are increasingly discussed not only as machines but also as a potential technological population. We develop a nonlinear population-dynamical framework to examine their possible diffusion relative to humans, without assuming that large-scale adoption or numerical crossover is inevitable. The human population $H(t)$ is calibrated to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 median trajectory. The android population $A(t)$ is represented through the normalized stock $a=A/A_s$. A conventional, human-organized manufacturing and adoption channel is calibrated to a conditional scenario spanning approximately $10^4$ humanoids in 2025 to $10^9$ in 2050 and follows $\dot a=(q_M+r_Ma)\exp(K_Ma^\gamma)$. We separately introduce a hypothetical autonomous channel in which installed androids contribute materially to producing additional androids. Under the minimal canonical TZ closure, the corresponding production--feedback number is $\mathcal{P}(a)=(r_A/\delta_A)\exp(K_Ra)$, where $r_A$ is the gross robot-mediated production coefficient, $\delta_A$ the retirement rate, and $K_R$ the autonomous feedback parameter. This channel is locally self-amplifying if and only if $\mathcal{P}>1$, whereas numerical human--android parity, $A=H$, is a separate cumulative condition. Global uncertainty analysis shows that crossover dates remain strongly scenario-dependent, while the production--feedback threshold is more robust. An extreme early-autonomy stress test can produce parity by 2050, but this represents a conditional dynamical boundary rather than a technological forecast.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Zaccone, Thomas Tunstall, Jesse H. Ausubel

item.title: Inferring missing locations in human mobility data using memory effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.01319v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Empirical datasets used to characterize human mobility are sparse in space and time, owing to technological factors such as coverage and battery, or to the erratic nature of online interactions. Missing data can bias the conclusions drawn from them, so filling the gaps in incomplete timelines is a key challenge in computational social science. Here, we propose a simple imputation method in which the informativeness of an observation decays with its bidirectional temporal distance from the missing entry, at a rate set by a single parameter per individual. On synthetic and real Twitter data, a power-law decay, selected by Bayesian model comparison, yields accurate imputations (macro-AUROC above 0.9 overall, and above 0.8 for the most mobile users) and matches a gap-aware continuous-time Markov chain, outperforming it among the most mobile users. The method is robust to moderate noise and generalizes across countries and European administrative regions.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Rosillo-Rodes, Ant\`onia Tugores, David S\'anchez, Jos\'e J. Ramasco

item.title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
item.description: arXiv:2611.01750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Herfindahl--Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration, is widely used to quantify competitive balance in sports tournaments. To enable comparisons over time or across leagues, both its minimum and maximum should be known. The minimum is usually trivial. Our paper provides results on the maximum HHI in incomplete round-robin tournaments, where the set of matches is represented by a regular but not complete undirected graph. We prove that the lower bound of maximum HHI is reached when the tournament consists of independent round-robin groups, while the upper bound of maximum HHI is reached when the set of matches is represented by a bipartite graph. Maximising HHI is computationally difficult even for highly structured graph types corresponding to real-world tournaments, where the teams are partitioned into pots and play the same number of matches against opponents from every pot. The complexity of the problem does not depend on the scoring system or the number of opponents from a pot.
item.dc:creator: Gergely Cs\'aji, L\'aszl\'o Csat\'o

item.title: AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.01918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback. In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes. The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility
item.dc:creator: Jiaheng Xiao, Jiangtao Han, Jiachen Wang, Honghai Li, Lijun Sun, Kay Axhausen, Chang Liu, Zhengbing He

item.title: When Does Triadic Balance Reduce to Pairwise Order?
item.description: arXiv:2611.02117v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structural-balance interactions are naturally defined on triads, but when pair affinities are themselves generated by continuous node attributes, it is not clear whether the resulting interaction remains genuinely higher order. Here we address this question for agents represented by unit vectors in an attribute space, with pair affinity given by their scalar product and a Heider product assigned to each triangle. For planar attributes, we show that the triadic interaction reduces exactly, at finite system size, to a pairwise Curie--Weiss XY model of the doubled angles. The ordered phase is therefore nematic and undergoes a continuous mean-field $O(2)$ transition at $k_{\mathrm B}T_c=J/8$. The same reduction reveals a local $\mathbb Z_2$ degeneracy: each nematically ordered state corresponds to $2^N$ polar assignments, whose binomial multiplicities make two nearly equal opposite groups typical at low temperature. Monte Carlo simulations support the exact critical temperature, the mean-field Binder-cumulant value, and the predicted complete-graph finite-size scaling. Finally, a tensor representation of the interaction shows that the planar reduction is dimension specific: in two dimensions the cubic invariant is constrained by lower-order invariants, whereas for $d\geq3$ it is generically independent. These results identify when attribute-induced triadic balance is effectively pairwise and when genuinely higher-order structure can remain.
item.dc:creator: Sepideh Arab Mohammadi, Amir Kargaran, Ali Hosseiny, Reza Jafari, Abbas Ali Saberi

item.title: Beating the average: how to generate profit by exploiting the inefficiencies of soccer betting
item.description: arXiv:2303.16648v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In economy, markets are denoted as efficient when it is impossible to systematically generate profits which outperform the average. In the past years, the concept has been tested in other domains such as the growing sports betting market. Surprisingly, despite its large size and its level of maturity, sports betting shows traits of inefficiency. The anomalies indicate the existence of strategies which shift betting from a game of chance towards a game of skill. This article shows an example for an inefficiency detected in the German soccer betting TOTO 13er Wette, which is operated by state-run lottery agencies. Gamblers have to guess the outcome (win, draw, loss) of 13 soccer matches listed on a lottery tip. Applying stochastic methods, a recipe is presented to determine hit rates for single match outcomes. More important, the recipe provides the number of lottery tips required to achieve a specific number of strikes (number of correct match forecasts per lottery tip) for any given level of safety. An approximation is derived to cope with large numbers in hypergeometric distributions, valid under certain constraints. Overall, the strategy does lead to returns exceeding the aggregated lottery fees, resulting in moderate, but consistent profits. It is briefly discussed if lessons learned from soccer betting can be transferred back to financial markets, because gamblers and retail investors face similar challenges and opportunities.
item.dc:creator: Ralph St\"ommer

item.title: Unbeatable imitation of a friend
item.description: arXiv:2507.16221v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Imitation sometimes achieves success in multi-agent situations even though it is very simple. In repeated games, success of imitation has been characterized by unbeatability against other agents. Previous studies specified conditions under which imitation is unbeatable against co-players in repeated symmetric games, and clarified that the existence of unbeatable imitation is strongly related to the existence of payoff-controlling strategies, called zero-determinant strategies. However, these results were on the situations in which one repeated game is played by one group of players. It was pointed out that imitation of other players in the same group and imitation of other players in the same role in other groups generally result in different outcomes. Here, we investigate the existence condition of unbeatable imitation in the latter situations, described by two concurrent repeated games played by two different groups of players. We find that the existence condition of unbeatable imitation is stronger than the existence condition of unbeatable zero-determinant strategies, whereas both are very limited. Furthermore, we find that adding exploration can make an imitation strategy unbeatable even in games where imitation without exploration can be beaten. Our findings suggest a strong relation between unbeatable imitation and payoff control even in the two concurrent repeated game situations.
item.dc:creator: Masahiko Ueda

item.title: Collective evolutionary dynamical-systems games: Emergent turn-taking under anonymous monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2507.22555v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sustainable resource use in large societies requires institutions that define and enforce acceptable behaviour while keeping monitoring costs manageable. Here we show that such institutions can arise even when users observe only anonymised group-level information. Using the evolutionary dynamical-systems game framework, we model a common-pool resource management game. In the model, each player's harvesting decisions depend on the resource abundance, the player's wealth, and the group-average wealth. Strategies are encoded as two-parameter decision-making functions that mutate across generations. Evolutionary simulations reveal that players self-organise into clusters that alternate harvesting turns. A simple rule emerges, wait when wealthy, harvest when below average, which generates turn-taking patterns and robustness against selfish overharvesters. While the majority cluster tends to exploit the minority, moderate diversity in strategies allows "turn-taking of turns" between the majority and minority roles, improving efficiency, equity, and robustness. Moderate stochasticity in both resource dynamics and peer monitoring can enhance efficiency. The conditions for sustaining these institutions depend strongly on group size and demographic history. Gradual group expansion allows sustainability at substantially larger group sizes. These results provide a mechanistic account of the self-organisation of institutions under anonymous monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Kenji Itao, Kunihiko Kaneko

item.title: How Withheld Punishment Sustains Anti-Democratic Behavior in an Evolutionary Game
item.description: arXiv:2512.06245v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Democratic backsliding is often framed as a contest between defenders and disruptors of democratic institutions. That framing can miss a third response, withholding punishment from disruptors while penalizing defenders who confront them. We model the three responses as strategies in an evolutionary game, track their shares with replicator dynamics, and assume defenders beat disruptors head-to-head but have a payoff disadvantage among non-punishers even when disruptors are absent. If the third response cannot spread among disruptors, a payoff condition draws the population toward the classical May--Leonard heteroclinic cycle, a rock--paper--scissors succession in which disruption repeatedly becomes rare, then widespread. If that response can, a threshold on its payoff advantage over disruptors determines whether all three coexist or defenders alone vanish. In finite-population simulations, sustained resurgence requires reintroducing lost strategies. Our contribution is to show how two separately documented political tendencies, if combined, can sustain disruption despite defenders' head-to-head advantage over disruptors.
item.dc:creator: Chad M. Topaz

item.title: Boundary crossings as a minimal mechanism for global connectivity in structured landscapes
item.description: arXiv:2606.07344v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Global connectivity in complex systems often emerges from local interactions, yet it remains unclear whether sophisticated agent strategies are required for such reorganisation. Here we identify a minimal mechanism by which heterogeneous mobility can generate system-wide connectivity when agents move within a structured multi-attractor landscape. In an agent-based model, a small fraction of higher-mobility agents explores the environment while the majority remains locally constrained. Configurational transitions are strongly localised at inter-attractor boundaries, where local crossing events accumulate over time to produce an expanding transition network and a percolation-like shift from fragmented to globally connected regimes. The core phenomenon persists under pure random-walk dynamics, showing that neither optimisation nor goal-directed behaviour is necessary. Interface-sensitive exploration nevertheless increases the transition rate by approximately four- to fivefold per exploratory movement relative to the random-walk baseline, thereby accelerating network integration. A novelty term produces only a small and non-uniform additional rate increase and no consistent improvement in unique-edge production. By contrast, when landscape structure is removed, transition-network connectivity arises through unconstrained spatial mixing, eliminating the boundary-mediated interpretation of the process. These results identify a minimal mechanism through which simple stochastic movement and spatial constraints generate large-scale connectivity. Interfaces between basins emerge as critical mediators linking local dynamics to global organisation, with potential implications for systems in which movement occurs across structured environments.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Nelli

item.title: Detecting Historical Turning Points in Italian Media: A Complex Systems Approach to a Diachronic News Corpus
item.description: arXiv:2606.14348v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Introduction: The increasing availability of large-scale textual corpora has opened new possibilities for data-driven, quantitative approaches to historical analysis using Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, diachronic corpora with historical relevance from the pre-digital era remain scarce and often incomplete. Methods: We present a quantitative approach to historical analysis based on the reconstruction and exploration of a diachronic corpus of around 600,000 articles from the Italian newspaper "La Repubblica", covering all the articles published from the first of January 1985 to the 31st of December 2000 - a period of major political, social, and geopolitical change in Italy and globally. Using NLP techniques, we analyze the text at both lexical and semantic levels; we then apply tools from complex systems and statistical physics to trace shifts in media discourse over time. Results: The word usage in the corpus is bursty, with a heavy-tailed distribution of Fano factors that is robust across timescales. Changepoints in word salience and the block structure of semantic similarity allow us to detect key transition periods, such as the transition from the First Republic to the Second Republic in Italy, or major international conflicts like the Gulf War or the Kosovo War, without relying on prior labeling. Periods of war correspond to lower entropy in the semantic space, indicating a more focused discourse. Discussion: The results show how combining computational linguistics with ideas from complex systems can offer new quantitative insight into historical changes, opening up new paths for studying the dynamics of media and society through large-scale textual data.
item.dc:creator: Dario Zarcone, Salvatore Miccich\`e, David Sanchez

item.title: Early warning signals for synchronization transitions from partial observations
item.description: arXiv:2608.28320v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Anticipating the onset of collective synchronization is important in many networked systems, yet observing every oscillator is often impractical. We investigate whether synchronization transitions can be detected from a small set of monitored, or sentinel, nodes. Using a stochastic Kuramoto model on networks, we numerically compare three early warning signals: the local order parameter, its temporal variance, and the variance of individual oscillator phases after removing their mean rotational trends. We also compare sentinel-selection strategies based on node dynamics, degree, and random sampling. We show that, under partial observation, the local order parameter and the variance of detrended phases provide substantially stronger warning signals than the variance of the local order parameter. Selecting nodes according to their dynamical behavior near the transition consistently improves performance over other sentinel-selection methods. With only $\lfloor\ln N\rfloor$ dynamically selected sentinels, two success indicators approach the performance obtained by observing all $N$ nodes. These results demonstrate that synchronization transitions can be anticipated from sparse observations when the warning signal and monitored nodes are chosen appropriately.
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Kato, Naoki Masuda

item.title: Hybrid epidemic simulation framework coupling equation-based and individual-based models
item.description: arXiv:2609.35162v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mass gathering events (MGEs) can create intense, short-lived transmission hotspots whose effects propagate through urban populations. Quantifying these effects requires linking fine-scale interactions during gatherings with epidemic transmission across metropolitan mobility networks. We developed a hybrid multiscale simulation framework coupling empirically derived individual-based contact networks for MGEs with a stochastic metapopulation susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered (SEIR) model. Using population and commuting data from Madrid, Spain, we investigated how event-related transmission affects epidemic dynamics and district-level invasion. Across the scenarios examined, MGEs increased epidemic peak incidence and accelerated epidemic progression, although the magnitude of these effects depended on event-specific contact patterns and background transmissibility. Dense contact patterns produced greater epidemic amplification, whereas measures reducing close-contact interactions weakened these effects. MGEs also advanced epidemic invasion across districts and increased the temporal synchronization of arrival times, producing a more synchronized metropolitan epidemic wave. The association between MGEs and earlier district-level invasion was partly explained by the size of the event-generated epidemic seed. The main patterns persisted across the epidemiological parameter ranges examined. The framework provides a multiscale approach for investigating how mass gathering management may influence metropolitan epidemic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Jaeyoung Kwak, Michael H. Lees, Chin Chun Ooi, Wentong Cai

item.title: Settlement percolation reveals shrinking critical distances across the urban hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2610.37073v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measures of urban expansion quantify land consumption but obscure how separated settlements coalesce. We examine India's 50 largest urban agglomerations (1975-2025) using percolation-like analysis. Critical distances marking the largest settlement-merger events contracted in 47 cities, the median falling 46% from 650 to 350m. This longitudinal shrinking of settlement connectivity length scales reveals a morphological mechanism shaping land-consumptive settlement growth through distinct forms of inter-cluster coalescence (compact, corridor, satellite, regional). Population size shows no detectable linear relationship with contraction magnitude, although intermediate-sized agglomerations display the widest observed spread. Confirming established land-consumption patterns, built-up surfaces and urban footprints grow faster than population. Yet their relative growth flips with urban delineation: before the largest merger, footprints outgrow built-up surface (386% versus 361%); immediately afterward, built-up surface outgrows footprints (315% versus 287%). Recognizing merger dynamics can guide infrastructure investment, prioritize sustainable infill, reduce land consumption, and protect agricultural and ecologically sensitive landscapes.
item.dc:creator: Somwrita Sarkar, Chirag Deb, Carolina Pantoja Mardones, Anmol Gaur, Arunim Anand, Rashi Shrivastava, Anusha Roy, Arnab Jana, Eswar Rajasekaran, David Levinson

item.title: Soccer: a quantitative analysis of team resilience and the miracle of Bern
item.description: arXiv:2203.06933v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Resilience is the ability to positively respond to adversity. It has been studied in psychology for several decades, with focus on how individuals overcome traumata or cope with setbacks and obstacles in their professional career. Research on resilience in the sport context is rather new. Activities are based on insights that in highly competitive environments, tiny effects tip the scales. A key question of measuring resilience in sports is what parameters to measure. Here a novel concept is proposed to measure the resilience of soccer teams. The relative frequency of matches is determined, where a soccer team, which is initially trailing by 2 goals, finally succeeds to win the match or at least to reach a draw. The analysis is applied to the last 59 seasons of the German premier soccer league Bundesliga. The empirical data are compared with a theoretical model derived from Poisson distributions. It is shown how leading teams in the premier soccer league differ from the average with respect to resilience, which provides further insights into the hidden secrets of top soccer teams.
item.dc:creator: Ralph St\"ommer

item.title: Do media narratives shape foreign ownership? Evidence from African regions
item.description: arXiv:2403.10239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foreign investors rarely observe local business conditions directly, especially in developing economies where reliable subnational information is limited. In such contexts, media narratives may shape how investment locations are perceived by increasing their visibility and framing local risks and opportunities. This paper examines the relationship between media narratives and foreign ownership across African locations. We combine firm-level data from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys with a novel corpus of 167,746 English-language news articles on industrial investment in Africa published between 2014 and 2019. Using text mining and semantic network analysis, we construct investment-location measures of the semantic importance of business-related media themes through the Semantic Brand Score (SBS) and study their associations with firm-level foreign ownership. The results point to a significant association between how the media frames a location and the level of foreign presence there. This association varies across frames. It is predominantly positive, relates to both the intensive and extensive dimensions of foreign ownership depending on the theme, and may interact negatively with the investment climate. This paper contributes to research on the geography of foreign capital by identifying public narratives as a feature of the information environment associated with observed foreign-equity participation.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Research in International Business and Finance, 92, 103681 (2026)
item.dc:creator: A. Fronzetti Colladon, R. Vestrelli, S. Bait, M. M. Schiraldi

item.title: Inferring Stochastic Dynamics Reveals Atypicality and Irreversibility in Social Change
item.description: arXiv:2601.17772v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human social systems bear striking similarities, yet similar conditions can give rise to markedly different historical trajectories. A central challenge for quantitative social science is therefore to use time-series data to identify features common to the evolution of different social systems without obscuring the variation distinguishing individual histories. Here, we address this challenge by fitting stochastic differential equations (SDEs) to ensembles of observed trajectories through spaces of socially relevant variables. Importantly, the SDE allows the average tendency and variability of change to depend on the current state of the system. This flexibility allows us to use the SDE to analyze myriad aspects of social dynamics. Specifically, the fitted SDEs identify regions of the state space where stochastic variability is greater, allowing a broader range of plausible subsequent changes. The fitted SDE also allows us to quantify the dynamical irreversibility of observed trajectories and how that irreversibility depends on the values of the social variables. In addition, we show how the SDEs can be used to identify statistically atypical transitions in individual trajectories, indicative of exogenous perturbations impacting the associated society. We apply these tools to three domains: modern political economy, quantitative history, and cultural analytics. This reveals state-dependent change in the organization of modern political-economic systems; a broad but stochastic tendency toward increasing social complexity in historical societies; and time-dependent reorganization of lexical dynamics in English. Looking forward, we argue that our framework provides a set of powerful quantitative tools that can be used to investigate a broader range of longitudinal social phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Youngkyoung Bae, Hajime Shimao, Seungwoong Ha, Luna Yang, David Wolpert
